1) Cystoid macular edema (CME) secondary to chronic anterior uveitis — Most likely. Unilateral fine keratic precipitates, 1+ AC cells and OCT-proven CME/subfoveal fluid match inflammatory CME from chronic anterior uveitis in a pseudophakic eye.
2) Pseudophakic (Irvine–Gass) cystoid macular edema — Very possible given history of IOLs; presentation can be subacute/chronic and causes similar OCT findings and decreased vision.
3) Herpetic (HSV/VZV) anterior uveitis with secondary CME — Possible: typically unilateral, can produce KPs, mild AC inflammation and resultant CME; consider if recurrent or steroid-responsive with IOP changes.
4) Retinal vascular cause of CME (e.g., branch retinal vein occlusion or macular ischemia) — Less likely given anterior segment inflammation, but can produce CME/subretinal fluid; needs posterior pole evaluation to rule out.
5) Chronic infectious or neoplastic posterior segment inflammation (e.g., indolent endophthalmitis, intraocular lymphoma) — Uncommon but important to consider if atypical course or poor response to therapy.

Suggested immediate next steps (for confirmation and management): dilated fundus exam with careful posterior segment evaluation and fundus photography, fluorescein angiography (or OCT-angiography) to characterize leakage pattern, and trial of anti-inflammatory therapy (topical steroid ± topical NSAID and cycloplegic) with close follow-up. If herpetic etiology is suspected or if CME is refractory, consider anterior chamber PCR for herpes viruses and/or referral for periocular or intravitreal steroid therapy.
